Bolivia holds the largest known lithium reserves on Earth. On this map of who actually produces it, Bolivia is almost blank.

One map, and a resource curse in slow motion — a thread 🧵🗺️

Data: Our World in Data (CC BY)

1/ The map shows lithium mine production in 2024. Australia leads at roughly 88,000 tonnes, mostly hard-rock spodumene. Chile follows at about 57,000 tonnes, then China around 41,000 — both drawing heavily on evaporated brine.

2/ Chile and Argentina pump brine from ancient salt flats — the Salar de Atacama, the Salar del Hombre Muerto — into ponds, let the sun evaporate the water, and skim off lithium-rich salts. Slow, but far cheaper than digging rock.

3/ Bolivia's Salar de Uyuni is the largest salt flat on the planet and sits on an enormous lithium resource. But its brine runs unusually high in magnesium, which fouls the extraction chemistry and makes isolating the lithium slower and costlier.

4/ Geology isn't the only obstacle. Bolivia has cycled through nationalized lithium projects, shifting state partners, and political instability since the 2000s — scaring off the foreign capital and expertise Chile and Argentina welcomed in.

5/ Australia's lead runs on a different playbook: mature mining law, infrastructure left over from decades of iron ore and coal extraction, and hard-rock deposits that convert to production far faster than brine ever can.

6/ China barely mines a third of what it processes. Its real power on this map is invisible — it refines most of the world's lithium into battery-grade material, whichever country the ore came from.
